quotes.text: Kim Wilde and her producer brother Ricky essentially gave the same makeover to the Supremes classic "You Keep Me Hangin' On," drenching it in keyboard flutters and distorto-guitar growls and big-boom drums.
As for Kim Wilde, she already had experience heralding the arrival of a new sound. Years earlier, she'd helped introduce the world to new wave.

"Kids In America" stands as an absolute classic of the synthy, self-aware pop music that flourished in the wake of punk rock -- a wistfully giddy banger about waiting around for better things to arrive.
Wilde Winter Songbook is a holiday album that includes both well-known Christmas songs and new compositions with a Christmas/Winter theme.

Musically, this is a piano-based track with some acoustic guitar and percussion in its arrangement. Near the end, though, the arrangement becomes fuller with the key change, and I love how this fits in with the song's theme of having hope, especially during the holiday season.
Musically, this one has a simple arrangement of just piano, strings, and Kim's vocals. I love the simplicity of the arrangement, as I think it helps to emphasize the emotion behind the lyrics.

Musically, the arrangement has a bit of a "hymn-like" quality, and the arrangement is on the minimal side for the majority of the track, which allows the vocals to be the overall focus of this recording.

There's a simplistic arrangement for most of the song, which evokes a feeling of a lullaby. The only exception is right near the end of the track, when more instruments are added and the arrangement picks up in intensity and then reaches a crescendo.

Musically, the arrangement evokes a feeling of winter and snow falling. For the "Burn Gold" portion of the song, the lyrics rely on tree imagery, especially the idea of the turning of the leaves' colors.
Musically, the album is mainly new wave and rock-oriented, but it also features a reggae track ("Everything We Know"), and a brass section appears on "2-6-5-8-0".

Lyrically, Marty Wilde included love songs and also a song ("Water on Glass") about tinnitus (a medical condition that causes ringing in the ears), a song about the deterioration of inner cities ("Our Town") and a song about a theory that sound is alive ("Tuning in Tuning On").

Eric Chappe called the album an "immediately striking disc", citing the "'60s girl group mannerisms" and "Spector-esque drum sound" of "Water on Glass" while drawing comparisons to both Dusty Springfield and Debbie Harry.

Record Mirror critic Mike Nicholls praised Wilde's voice and individuality despite comparing the reggae-influenced "Everything We Know" to "The Tide Is High" by Blondie, released the previous year. Calling "Tuning in Tuning On" a "clever closer", Nicholls suggested that the track provided "requisite experimentation" and could indicate a new synth-driven direction for the singer.
In interviews leading up to the release of Closer, Kim commented that the album was a kind of "follow-up" to her 1988 album, Close.
According to Ricky Wilde, the song's composition has similarities with "Kids In America," so I guess I wasn't hearing things.

According to Ricky and Kim, was originally written for the 2018 album, Here Come the Aliens, but it was decided that it just didn't quite work for how that album was shaping up. However, they liked the chorus so much that it was incorporated as an intro to the song "Solstice." When it came time to work on Closer, they decided to include "Lighthouse" on the album.

Musically, I thought it was taking some inspiration from the Teases & Dares era but bringing in a more modern feel to it. In some respects, the more modern elements feel as if they're taking some influence from EDM.
Musically, it feels like this one is taking inspiration from some of Kim's earliest material from the 1980's.

Ricky has commented that he was inspired by Depeche Mode musically for this song, and Kim stated that she had just read a poem by Alexei Navalny that he had written to his wife while in prison and was moved by it to write the lyrics to this song.
